title: Negotiation and compensation
subtitle: Read every part of a tech offer, know what equity and CTC really mean, and ask for more honestly, with data and without fear.

c.v: This story is made up. Asha and Vikram, backend engineers with three years of experience, pass the same loop at the same company. Each gets the same offer by phone: base salary, a bonus and "some stock".
Vikram is relieved and says yes on the call. He sees nothing in writing until the joining date.
Asha thanks them and asks for the offer by email. Then she asks: which level is this? What kind of stock is it, and how does it vest? Is there a sign-on bonus?

The stock vests over four years, with nothing in the first year. The level is one below the role she applied for. Asha asks what it was based on, and points to the design round she led. The level stays, but the company adds a sign-on bonus and more stock.
A year later, Vikram learns the difference. Same loop, same skills, different pay. He just never asked.
An offer is a set of parts, not one number. Each part has its own rules, risks and room to move.
Negotiation is a normal, polite talk about those parts.
The key idea.
Get the offer in writing, understand each part, and ask for what you need with real data. Never lie about other offers.
This lesson explains how offers work. It is not financial or tax advice. For big decisions, ask a qualified advisor.
The parts of a tech offer
Base salary.
Fixed pay, every month. It is the safest part.
Bonus.
Often a yearly target percentage of base. It depends on results, so it may not be paid in full.
Equity.
A share in the company, as
RSUs
or
stock options
. See below.
Sign-on bonus.
A one-time payment for joining. Ask if you must pay it back if you leave early.
Benefits.
Health insurance, leave and retirement plans.
RSUs and stock options
An RSU is a right to receive shares once
vesting
conditions are met. You own no shares on the grant date.
A stock option is the right, but not the duty, to buy shares at a fixed price, the
strike price
, after a vesting period. Startups often give options to employees as part of pay.
Both usually vest over time. GitLab's handbook describes a four-year schedule for new-hire stock options, with a
one-year cliff
. It says that "at most companies, including GitLab", the cliff is generally one year.
There, RSUs vest over two to four years from the grant date, and refresh grants have no cliff.
Step through a made-up option grant below.
At GitLab, unvested RSUs and options are lost when you leave. Vested options must be bought within 90 days of leaving.
Read your own grant agreement.
Why options can be worth nothing.
For traded options, Investor.gov explains that a call option is "out-of-the-money" when the strike price is above the share price.
Employee options are not traded, but in our reading the same sums apply. If the share price stays at or below your strike price, buying at that price gains you nothing.
Private shares add a second risk. An SEC staff explainer says startup shares are "often illiquid": you cannot easily sell them. Money usually comes at an exit, such as an IPO or an acquisition.
If a startup winds down, it pays its debts first. What is left goes to shareholders in order of liquidation preference.
So in your sums, count startup options as uncertain and possibly worth zero, not as salary. This is our advice.
In India: CTC versus in-hand pay
Indian offers often show
CTC
, the cost to company: the total the employer spends on you, not what reaches your bank.
It often includes:
Variable pay.
A bonus target that may be paid in part or not at all.
Employer PF.
EPFO says both employee and employer contribute 12% of basic wages plus dearness allowance.
In our experience, most offers put the employer's 12% inside CTC. Your own 12% comes out of your salary.
Gratuity.

A lump sum paid when you leave. Most permanent staff qualify only after five years of continuous service. The Code on Social Security, 2020 waives this for death, disablement or the end of a fixed-term contract.
Fixed-term staff qualify after one year.
The amount is 15 days' wages per year of service. For monthly pay, that is monthly wages ÷ 26 × 15.
These rules apply from 21 November 2025.
It may sit in CTC each year, but you get it only if you qualify.
Here is a made-up example. "Wages" here means basic pay plus dearness allowance. Under the new codes, if other pay is more than half the total, the excess counts as wages.
So assume wages of ₹12,00,000 a year, about half the pay.
CTC: ₹24,00,000 a year.
Variable pay: ₹2,40,000.
Insurance: ₹12,000.
After your own PF of ₹1,44,000: ₹18,02,300, about ₹1,50,000 a month before income tax.
EPFO makes contributions mandatory when basic pay plus DA is up to ₹15,000 a month, and voluntary above.
So employers calculate PF in different ways. Ask for a full salary breakup.
Where to find market data
As of 2026, these are common sites. In our experience:
levels.fyi
shows pay by company and level, shared by users.
Glassdoor
has salaries and company reviews posted by employees and job seekers.
Blind
is an anonymous forum where tech workers discuss pay and offers.
All three are mostly self-reported. We think people with high or unusual pay may post more often. Data can be old. Use a range from several sources.
Three ideas from negotiation research
BATNA
Your Best Alternative to a Negotiated Agreement is what you will do if this deal fails. PON says a deal should beat your BATNA, and interviewing at several firms makes it stronger.
Anchoring.
PON describes the
anchoring effect
: the first number tends to pull later offers towards it. Employers often name the first number, so plan for it.
Research your range before the call.
Interests, not positions.

A position is a fixed demand; an interest is the need behind it. In PON's job example, the company cares about its budget. A signing bonus instead of a raise, or a salary review tied to milestones, can still meet your need.
The script
Our suggested script:
Thank them and get it in writing.
"Thank you, I'm excited about this team. Could you email me the full offer?"
Ask for time.
"I'd like a few days to review it. Can I reply by Friday?"
Ask about every part.
Level, base, bonus target, equity type and vesting, sign-on, benefits, and in India the CTC breakup.
Ask about the level.
Level sets your pay band. The
interview loops lesson
explains how it is set.
Make one clear request.
"Based on market data and how my design round went, I'd ask for ₹X base. If base is fixed, could we look at the sign-on bonus?"
Use competing offers honestly.
Name a real offer only if you have it. Be ready to show it.
Never lie about another offer. Companies may ask for the letter. A lie can end a real offer, and it is wrong.
What is usually negotiable

In our experience, sign-on bonus and equity move most often. Base moves within the band for your level. The level itself moves only with evidence. Benefits and bonus percentages are usually fixed by policy.
Exploding offers
An exploding offer has a very short deadline, such as 24 hours. Our advice: politely ask for a few more days. If they refuse, still read every term before you decide.
Pay transparency laws
As of 2026, Colorado's Equal Pay for Equal Work Act requires employers to disclose pay in all job postings, internal and public. It also bans asking about your pay history.
Since 1 November 2022, New York City has required a "good faith pay range" in all job ads for work done in the city.
A posted range is useful data. But PON warns that an advertised range can anchor talks in the employer's favour, so do your own research too.
Raises and promotions inside your company
Internal pay follows your company's levels and review cycle. The later lesson on
career ladders
covers it.
Accept on the call
Less pay or a lower level than you could get.
Almost never.
Counter with market data
Low. The answer may be no.
Usually.
Counter with a real competing offer
They may decline to match.
You would really take the other offer.
Bluff about an offer you do not have
You can lose the offer and your name.
Never.
Simple rule:
understand every part, know your alternative, ask once with evidence, and stay honest.

sections.title: At work: how a senior uses this

c.v: Before a job search, write your BATNA in one line. "If this fails, I stay and aim for promotion in March."
Compare offers in the same terms. Turn equity into a yearly value, and mark private equity as uncertain.
As an interviewer, write clear level evidence. It helps candidates get the right level.
"Act as a polite but firm recruiter. Role-play the call while I ask about the level, vesting and a sign-on bonus. Then tell me where I was unclear."
"Here is my offer letter with names removed. List every pay component, the vesting schedule, any cliff, and any clause about paying back a bonus. Quote the exact lines."
Every number the agent reads from your letter, against the letter itself.
Tax and legal claims. Confirm them with official sources or an advisor.
Your script. Never ask the agent to invent a competing offer or fake data.
Privacy. Remove names, IDs and salary account details before you paste.

and

. Next: career ladders.

q.v: An offer has 4,800 stock options over 4 years with a 1-year cliff and monthly vesting after it. You leave after 18 months. About how many units have vested?

why.v: The cliff gives 1,200 at month 12. Then 100 a month for 6 months adds 600. 1,200 + 600 = 1,800.

q.v: A startup offers you stock options with a strike price of ₹100 a share. Which statement is true?

options.v: The options are worth at least ₹100 a share.
They are worth something only if the share price rises above ₹100 and you can sell the shares.
They turn into cash every year, like a bonus.

why.v: An option lets you buy at the strike price. It has value only above that price, and private shares are often hard to sell until an exit.

q.v: Your Indian offer says "CTC ₹24 lakh". What should you ask first?

options.v: Nothing. CTC is the money paid into your bank account.
How much is fixed, how much is variable, and what is inside it, such as PF and gratuity.
Whether the CTC can be paid in cash.

why.v: CTC usually includes the variable bonus and employer costs such as PF. Your monthly in-hand pay is lower.

q.v: You have no other offer. The recruiter asks if you have one. What do you do?

options.v: Say you have one, to get a better number.
Say no, and use market data and your interview results to make your case.
Refuse to answer and end the call.

why.v: Never invent an offer. Use honest data and your interests instead. A made-up offer can cost you the real one.

q.v: In negotiation terms, what is your BATNA during a job offer?

options.v: The highest number you plan to ask for.
What you will do if this deal does not happen, such as staying in your job or taking another offer.

why.v: PON explains BATNA as your best alternative, what you will do if this deal fails. A stronger alternative lets you ask with more confidence.
